articles.title: If AOC Doesn’t Run for President, Run a Union Worker
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content: What do we do if Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez decides not to run for president in 2028? It makes sense that many leftists are currently focused on calling on her to take the plunge. But the absence of a Plan B, or even much discussion about one, is worrisome. The US left can’t afford to sit out the 2028 Democratic primary. Doing so in 2024 was a disaster: our abstention self-marginalized anti-billionaire politics from the national conversation and thereby gave space for Harris to pivot to the “center” (i.e., to the policy preferences of corporate donors, establishment hacks, and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee [AIPAC]). Abstaining again in 2028 would be especially counterproductive since democratic socialists now have so much wind in our sails after our big electoral wins in New York City and across the country. It’s time to deepen our momentum, organization, and profile — not to retreat to the margins during America’s single most important political battle. Even more urgently, keeping Donald Trump’s heir out of the White House may depend on whether leftists and the party’s unprecedentedly disenchanted base can force the Democrats in 2028 to take meaningful steps toward a very angry electorate and away from the corporate-consultant blob that has helped get us into this mess. If AOC (or Abdul El-Sayed ) decides to run, we should enthusiastically go all in — Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), fighting unions, progressive organizations, anybody who wants to see a better country and world. But, as far as I can tell from the outside, there’s a real chance that she doesn’t run. And we can’t just wait and see where she lands before discussing alternatives, since AOC’s decision might not come for quite a while, giving us little time to scramble at the last minute for an alternative. So we should start working now on getting a Plan B into motion, and recruiting a good candidate for the role. Here’s one idea. A Worker Candidate — Health Care, Not Warfare 2028 Run a union worker . Leftists don’t need to always run experienced, well-known socialist politicians for high-profile contests. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the current president of Brazil, began his political career as a metalworker militant who ran for governor of São Paulo in 1982. Especially in an era of institutional distrust, it’s possible to lean hard into making a virtue out of a working-class comrade’s distance from traditional politics. Experience abroad shows this clearly. Rachel Keke — an immigrant hotel housekeeper — ran as the candidate of the leftist La France Insoumise for the National Assembly in 2022, defeating a former minister in the Emmanuel Macron government. The Belgian Workers’ Party in 2024 won its first Flemish seat in the European Parliament by running Rudi Kennes , a three-decade veteran of the Opel Antwerp auto factory. And the South Korean left in 2024 elected auto factory militant Yoon Jong-oh to the National Assembly. If a tiny French Trotskyist organization could make such a big splash in 2002 and 2007 by running a well-spoken postal worker cadre for office — the Ligue Communiste Révolutionnaire’s Olivier Besancenot received about 1.5 million first-round votes — it’s not far-fetched to expect that a much larger organization like DSA, together with a broader coalition of the willing, could run this playbook to much greater effect. This is especially the case now that almost everything DSA does immediately becomes a national news story. We don’t need someone famous. We just need a charismatic, well-vetted comrade who works in a relatable working-class occupation — e.g., a nurse or a worker in auto, in construction, or at Amazon. Ideally, they have a compelling personal story or have been part of a significant strike or organizing campaign, but even those criteria don’t necessarily have to be deal-breakers. The main lesson of the Graham Platner fiasco isn’t that we should never run outsiders for office (the momentum he generated proves the exact opposite), but that they need proper vetting and roots in democratic membership organizations like DSA or a union. In any case, there are plenty of ways to signal working-class authenticity without resorting to Platner’s or John Fetterman’s performative macho-white-dude affect. Better to have someone of any gender or race who is actually working class, with firm socialist politics, who can speak from experience about the day-to-day realities of trying to make it in America. There are surely at least a dozen such worker leaders in our movement nationwide; we just need to sit down and convince one that their personal sacrifice for the greater good (i.e., running for president) will be worth it. If we don’t have a front-runner with a clear path to victory like AOC (or El-Sayed, were he to win Michigan), it’s better to embrace someone whose decision to run in itself tells an important story about US politics: workers have been iced out of our political system and are now fighting hard to break back in. The novelty factor, in itself, would generate press. And it would help democratic socialists signal to the American public that our movement’s defining characteristic is that we represent workers versus bosses, not that we’re “the furthest left” force in American politics — a framework that suggests we’re extremists, and that helps our opponents isolate us from non-college-educated voters by highlighting extremely minoritarian (and misguided ) stances included in DSA’s platform like prison abolition. We don’t get many opportunities to speak to tens of millions of Americans; we need to use these opportunities to broaden our appeal beyond those already in our orbit. Run to polarize the 2028 primary and general election around “Medicare for All” and “End all aid to Israel.” Why should democratic socialists use our scarce time and volunteer energy to run in a race we’re unlikely to win? Running in the 2028 primary will not only recruit us scores of members (imagine having a DSA member intervening in eleven nationally televised primary debates!), but — more importantly — it has the potential to be a decisive leap forward toward an America that finally starts meeting the needs of working people instead of HMO and AIPAC billionaire donors. Polarizing litmus tests are good, actually — as long as they’re fought for around popular demands in a thoughtful and strategic way. Democratic socialists have an opportunity and responsibility to make the 2028 primary about two of the most widely and deeply felt issues of our moment: domestically, America’s unaffordable, family-breaking private health care system; internationally, America’s bankrolling of the genocidal Israeli government. A candidacy relentlessly demanding Medicare for All (M4A) and “No aid to Israel” would pose a sharp question to the American public, the Democratic Party, and other 2028 contenders: Why can’t working-class Americans afford their health care bills at the same time that our government is spending at least $3.8 billion yearly to fund an Israeli regime eager to keep dragging us and the world into more forever wars? Our candidate can agitate around a clear message: I’m running to give voice to all those working-class Americans who are struggling to get by. No matter what state you live in, who you voted for in 2024, or your background, it’s just plain common sense that we should make health care more affordable instead of spending billions to enable the Israeli government’s crimes against humanity. Every American who agrees with me when I say ‘Medicare for All — Not a dime for Israel’ should make their voice heard through our campaign. Racking up a high number of votes for this agenda is a crucial way to show the Democratic Party and the country as a whole that we can’t keep supporting a life-destroying status quo in our health care system and in the Middle East. If we want to defeat Trump’s handpicked crony this coming November, we need to speak to ordinary people’s frustrations with the status quo — we can’t keep running the same tired establishment playbook and expecting a different result. For those highly engaged voters (or skeptical media pundits) who raise concerns about wasting votes, the candidate can take the time to explain why this isn’t the case: It’s true I’m a long shot. But Zohran Mamdani showed anything can happen — and voting for me is a pragmatic decision, not a wasted vote. In a heavily divided primary with a large number of candidates and a very discredited establishment, my campaign and the democratic socialist movement I’m part of are positioned to be the balance of power if we can get a large enough number of voters to loudly demand “Health care, not warfare.” Since there’s a high chance no candidate will get to 50 percent in the 2028 primaries, the Democrats could very well be heading toward a brokered convention , where a disciplined, principled current committed to breaking from corporate donors can play an outsize role in making sure whoever ends up with the nomination raises the banner of single-payer health care and cutting aid to Israel. How exactly could running this sort of primary campaign be translated into actual leverage? The candidate replies: I’m aiming to win the nomination, but if I don’t achieve that goal, my delegates and I will pledge our support in the primary only for a candidate who agrees in the general election to call for ending US aid to Israel and establishing Medicare for All at home. These are both winning planks for November against the Republicans, and the only reason I can see that other candidates haven’t yet raised these is that they’re still more scared of the donor class than they are of the people. That needs to change. If Democratic leaders want young people, workers, and those sick of the status quo to show up in big numbers this November, they need to meet us halfway. In this way, whether or not we win the nomination, democratic socialists could still play a decisive role in 2028. The approach outlined here is similar to what radical left parties periodically do in parliamentary democracies like Denmark or Sweden when they find themselves as a junior partner electorally: they dictate to center-left allies what their terms would be for enabling, from the outside, the formation of a new government. Running a “Health care, not warfare” candidate will make it significantly more likely that the 2028 Democratic candidate stands with ordinary people instead of donors on these two pivotal planks — a shift that will, in turn, make it easier to achieve the existentially important task of defeating MAGA’s heir in November. Look at how much popular traction the Uncommitted movement got with a similar strategy in 2024 with so little on-the-ground organization — surely we can go much further with a working-class candidate, a much bigger DSA, and a Democratic Party base that has turned against Israel, billionaires, and the hacks in the party who prop them up. Objections and Responses There are quite a few objections to this proposal, many of which are very reasonable. Let me briefly address each here. Socialists shouldn’t waste their scarce time and resources on a candidate unlikely to win . This is a good rule in general, but there are important exceptions, and presidential elections are the main one. There’s no other political contest that gets anything like this level of attention and engagement in the United States, so if you want to be a serious force in nationwide politics, you basically can’t afford not to have a candidate. Far from being an overall drain on our resources, running a dynamic 2028 campaign would likely result in a major net increase in members and capacity. In that spirit, the very pragmatic Milwaukee sewer socialists — who mostly ran to win at home in Wisconsin — supported Eugene Debs’s propagandistic presidential campaigns, which they correctly saw as a crucial means of recruiting to the Socialist Party. And now that the ( post-1972 ) Democratic Party gives more weight to voters than party operatives in determining its presidential nomination, it’s become feasible to run as a socialist in primaries without risking a split in the vote against the Republicans in November. We should just support Ro Khanna, who also supports M4A and ending aid to Israel . I like Ro Khanna and would enthusiastically vote and canvass for him for president were he to get the nomination. But there’s a real chance that Khanna’s bid for office doesn’t catch on; he lacks the grassroots organizational apparatus of DSA, and, because he’s not really of the Left or labor (despite his current very good positions), he’s unlikely to generate the type of buy-in and enthusiasm that a DSA candidate would. Moreover, Khanna would be running as an individual, not as someone emerging from and building an organized movement — his campaign would not likely focus on building sustained power from below, nor would it likely polarize the 2028 primary around M4A and Israel aid. Also, and not inconsequentially, the poor electoral results for Tom Steyer and Saikat Chakrabarti this spring suggest that there’s perhaps not much of a popular appetite in the Democrats’ base to support multimillionaire class traitors. Much better, then, to run a democratic socialist worker. If by Super Tuesday it’s clear that our campaign has captured the main left lane in the primary, Khanna should drop out and endorse us; conversely, if he’s managed to capture this lane, DSA could at that point transform its “Health care, not warfare” campaign into an independent campaign to elect Ro Khanna focused on winning (and holding him accountable to) those two critical planks. An openness to consolidating an anti-corporate candidate by Super Tuesday is a necessary component of the strategy I’m proposing, because otherwise we risk splitting the primary votes (per Democratic National Committee rules, you need at least 15 percent to get any delegates to convention). We should convince Shawn Fain or Sara Nelson to run for president instead . I agree it’d be great if either ran for president, but my impression is that there’s basically no chance that will happen in 2028, because both are firmly focused on their union leadership duties (and, in the case of Fain, beating back a federal witch hunt ). This plan could have DSA end up endorsing a nonsocialist, non-DSAer for president. That’s against our principles . It’s a myth, and bad politics, that socialists can’t ever support candidates who aren’t members of their organization and/or who don’t call themselves socialists. Bernie Sanders, after all, was not a DSAer. And socialists abroad regularly make tactical decisions about if and when supporting a nonsocialist candidate makes sense from the standpoint of promoting working-class interests, defending democracy, and building a socialist current in the process. If your “principles” prevent you and DSA from helping achieve the momentous stride forward of having a Democratic candidate in 2028 run on Medicare for All and ending aid to Israel, those “principles” are not very good. In fact, they actively undermine the causes they’re aiming to support. We shouldn’t confuse principles (working-class independence) with tactics (the best way to advance this in a given context). In my recent article in Catalyst on Milwaukee sewer socialism (I’ve uploaded the full text here ), I have a section showing how similarly rigid rules about endorsements had to be eventually discarded in the old Socialist Party nationwide after World War I because they tended to lead socialists toward a sectarian abstention from broader anti-corporate electoral insurgencies beyond their party’s control. For what it’s worth, Vladimir Lenin’s current under tsarism frequently backed bourgeois candidates in the second round of elections, and Lenin himself advocated that British Communists support Labour Party candidates; for his part, Karl Kautsky in 1912 defended the German Social Democracy’s electoral pact with the Progressives in the runoffs. If our predecessors could be that tactically flexible in an era before the limits of their underlying strategic assumptions about intransigent class politics in capitalist democracies were made clear , then there’s no need to insist on being more tactically rigid today, after a century’s worth of accumulated experience . As long as you maintain your own political profile and organization while engaging in broader coalitional efforts, there’s zero inherent contradiction with the principle of political independence. More specifically: DSA and allied organizations should enthusiastically back Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed if AOC declines to run and he throws his hat in the presidential ring. (I have no idea whether he’s even considering this path, but there’ll surely be chatter about it if he wins his Senate race this November.) Though he doesn’t call himself a socialist, El-Sayed is a principled Berniecrat, a consistent fighter for Palestine, and would have a clear path to victory. Using the S-word is far less important than whether a campaign fights for the interests of working people at home and abroad — and whether actively participating in it can grow the organized working class and the Left. And the same holds true if a less anti-corporate candidate were, under pressure, to adopt our two “Health care, not warfare” planks. Why focus only on M4A and ending US aid to Israel? There are so many other important issues to fight for ! Obviously there are many pivotal issues beyond health care and Israel, and our candidate — and especially our organizations involved in the campaign — should be prepared to speak on all of these. But one of the crucial lessons of the Zohran campaign is that you have to relentlessly stay on message if you want to cut through the noise. CNN and Fox News will want to talk about DSA’s views on Venezuela and abolishing the police; we need to polarize the debate on the widely and deeply felt issues that are most favorable for growing the Left, isolating our opponents, and winning urgently needed changes. One recent poll found 63 percent of Americans support M4A, even after respondents were told it would raise taxes and eliminate most private insurance. Another found that 74 percent of Democrats opposed “providing additional economic and military support to Israel.” And focusing on two demands sets the campaign up to be able to leverage its mandate to make clear demands upon other candidates (which we can’t do if we run with a laundry list of demands). Talking about a Plan B is a distraction from the more urgent work of building a groundswell of calls on AOC to run . It’s good for DSAers, fight-back unionists, and progressive organizations to try to convince AOC to run. This proposal is meant as an addendum to pushes to get AOC to run and to line DSA up for that eventuality, not as a substitute for those efforts. But I’m worried that, like in 2024, we might eventually find ourselves with no time to find a viable alternative unless we start now. DSA, with its abundant deliberative processes, moves slowly. The approach you’re suggesting seems risky. If a DSA candidate runs but doesn’t receive a lot of votes, it’ll undercut our current national momentum . This is a reasonable worry. All big initiatives always carry risks, and the path I’m advocating is certainly not free of these. That said, if a “Health care, not warfare” campaign doesn’t catch on like we envisioned, it’s a pretty simple pivot in March 2028 to explain that in the future we really need our standard-bearers like AOC, or our growing bench of national electeds, to step up in presidential primaries. Moreover, it’s worth noting that the risk of my Plan B proposal is on the whole significantly less than the risk entailed by an AOC run. We should all back her if she runs, since she’d fire up the base, provide huge openings for organizing, have a real shot at defeating a Republican (especially given MAGA’s unpopularity), be a great standard-bearer for our issues, particularly M4A and ending aid to Israel, and be less willing than mainstream candidates to capitulate to any antidemocratic machinations from Trump and co. But it’s also true that AOC could lose, which would be a devastating setback to the country and to the Left. Or she could win and find herself unable to pass much, if any, of her (and our) program, a demoralizing prospect. So if we’re willing to take these risks with AOC (and we should), it follows that we should be able to take lower-level risks if she doesn’t throw her hat in the ring. What’s Your Plan B? The US left is facing its biggest opening for growth and influence since the 1930s. Initiatives that would have been impossible a few months ago are now potentially feasible. A President AOC is now easier to imagine, but if she ultimately assesses that the risks aren’t worth the potential reward in 2028, we can’t be left flat-footed. So even if you’re not convinced by the specifics of my Plan B, I hope you can at least agree that it’d be a disaster for us not to have one — and not to start getting a Plan B into motion. Hopefully other organizers and political currents will put forward their responses and alternative ideas as soon as possible. The stakes are too high to just wait and see.

articles.title: Medicaid Cuts Could Kill Safety-Net Health Centers
articles.author: Maria Esch
articles.content: If you’ve ever driven through an American city, odds are you have seen a federally qualified health center (FQHC). FQHCs are safety-net medical providers dedicated to providing health services to people who may not otherwise have access to quality primary and outpatient care. According to one FQHC nurse, the facilities function to “fill gaps in our disaster of a health care system . . . and to address health disparity and provide health care to folks who just can’t be part of the capitalist health care system in America.”These clinics form the backbone of medical care for uninsured and underinsured Americans. In California alone, there are approximately 171 FQHCs and forty-three “look-alike” locations that function similarly but with key differences in their funding sources. In 2024, California FQHCS served nearly six million patients, 30 percent of whom are children, and the vast majority of whom live below the poverty line. Almost three-quarters of patients at these facilities received Medicaid benefits. Millions of Californians who may have otherwise been unable to receive medical care are supported by FQHCs.FQHCs are unique compared to other medical facilities, in that they receive about 9 percent of their funding from a federal 330 grant that requires clinics to follow a strict set of requirements on who they serve, how they spend money, and how their governing bodies are composed. (“Look-alike” clinics do not receive these federal grants but still serve a similar function to certified FQHCs.) The other 91 percent of funding for these facilities come from other sources, namely revenue from medical services provided. Since a majority of FQHC patients are insured by Medicaid, that program’s funding is a primary lifeline of these health centers.Donald Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1) proudly slashed vital Medicaid spending. Because of its passage, the program will lose almost $800 billion in federal dollars over the next ten years, and enrollment requirements will be much tighter. Together these changes are projected to reduce Medicaid enrollment by 10.3 million.These cuts begin a snowball effect. While the bill rips away health care access for millions of Americans, it also kneecaps health centers by cutting a major funding stream. According to one FQHC employee:It would be impossible for most of my patients to get health care without Medicaid. They’re just barely making it through, and so having Medicaid allows them to access care. I have no idea what they would do, how our clinic would survive, how patients would go on [without it].From there, the snowball continues downhill. Fewer patients will come in the door, eating away at the revenue stream from Medicaid. Lower revenue means closures at rural clinics, and fewer appointments mean people will need more emergency care when health issues reach a crisis point. Emergency Departments are required to serve the uninsured, and with higher volumes hospitals have to eat more of the cost of care.When hospitals lose funding, emergency departments are forced to close; nurses and support staff lose their jobs; equipment gets updated less frequently; wait times are longer; and remaining workers are stretched even thinner than they already are. Even people who don’t utilize Medicaid for their own health care will feel the effects of its budget-slashing.As of 2024, 79 percent of total functional expenses of California FQHCs go to program service expenses — things like staffing, patient care, and other spending used to further their community-oriented missions. There simply is not enough room in the budget to eat the enormous cost of lost Medicaid revenue.So how do FQHCs staunch the bleeding? In California, a solution has been proposed: the billionaire tax. So far, this proposal has been endorsed by California’s Democratic Party but denounced by Governor Gavin Newsom.California faces a loss of roughly $100 billion dollars in Medicaid funding over the next five years. With this onetime 5 percent tax on the wealth of Californians worth more than $1 billion, The tax would raise upward of $100 billion to “replace lost federal dollars and protect essential services,” as the proposal’s advocates put it. If passed, 90 percent of these funds will go to filling gaps in the health care budget lost to the Big Beautiful Bill, and 10 percent will go to food assistance and K–14 education.The money taken by a 5 percent wealth tax will barely be missed by the two hundred individual billionaires living in California, but it would mean the restoration of medical care for millions of poor and working-class Californians.Yet like Newsom, California FQHCs and other health care organizations are notably opposed to the proposition. The lack of support from FQHCs themselves is surprising, considering that this measure may be the only viable solution for keeping their organizations afloat.Across the country, Trump’s Medicaid cuts are primed to mortally wound federally qualified health centers and other health care providers. Unless something is done to fill the funding gap, and fast, we can expect a grim toll in human well-being and lives.

articles.title: Gen Z Can’t Go On. It Must Go On.
articles.author: David Moscrop
articles.content: Gen Z hates work . That seems fair enough, at least at first glance. At the same time, the CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, is complaining that his employees care more about their salaries than the company’s mission. That complaint is much harder to defend, but it inadvertently points to a broader question that relates to a growing culture of labor dropouts. Work has long been a source of individual expression, prosocial organization, and cooperation toward shared goals. Dismissing all labor out of hand as evil — or mere necessary toil — overlooks the distinction between work as purpose-driven human activity and wage labor as the exploitative, boss-driven form work takes under capitalism. Communities require work. And complex communities — such as any contemporary city, region, or state — require many different kinds of it. Much of this work is difficult and specialized. Much of it is not. But it is all essential to keeping the lights on. To say so isn’t to condone exploitation, low wages, or poor working conditions, nor is it to suggest that those who are unable to work ought not to be treated with dignity, respect, and care. Work as Civic Culture. Work as Alienation. Criticizing the labor market under capitalism is not only justifiable but rational and necessary. Opting out of the labor market in the face of exploitation is likewise justifiable. But it is a step down from organizing to change the conditions of work. As Albert O. Hirschman noted more than fifty years ago, beating a retreat can empower bosses by weakening the collective capacity of workers. “Exiting” the workplace entirely eventually leads to workers losing what he called “voice.” And in an age where the institutions that amplify workers’ voices — unions, cooperatives, workplace democracy — have already been weakened, the temptation to exit may be stronger than ever. Be that as it may, for the foreseeable future — artificial intelligence notwithstanding — human labor will be a nonnegotiable part of social life and the survival of the species. Workers would be better off if this labor was organized through a socialist economy rather than a capitalist one. But changing how work is coordinated is not the same as eliminating work altogether. A vibrant civic culture and the renewal of shared social purpose that we desperately need exists in part as a function of certain kinds of labor. Caring for the ill, teaching others, operating public transportation systems, running museums, growing food, writing books, collecting waste, and keeping facilities clean and accessible are forms of socially necessary labor we’d want under any economic system — even if the model of wage labor were altered. But we might not need all manners of, ah, work. Bertrand Russell captured the alienation of modern work in 1932 when he wrote that “Work is of two kinds: first, altering the position of matter at or near the earth’s surface relatively to other such matter; second, telling other people to do so.” Russell anticipated a critique that has now become commonplace. “The first kind is unpleasant and ill paid; the second is pleasant and highly paid,” he wrote. “The second kind is capable of indefinite extension: there are not only those who give orders but those who give advice as to what orders should be given.” Russel’s conception of labor captures the twentieth century’s turn toward managerial and professional work, as more labor — and eventually politics itself — moved to Madison Avenue. In the twenty-first century, there are plenty of astute contemporary critiques of labor under capitalism, most of which Karl Marx would have recognized. But iterations of the dropout sensibility based on perceptions that it takes a high-six-figure salary to find happiness, and that anything requiring more than a few hours a day and a laptop — or smartphone — is oppression miss the mark. The Return of Veblen’s Leisure Class Humans like to engage in socially useful undertakings. Low wages, exploitative working conditions, and the absence of worker control over workplaces alienate us from the social good of useful work. But so, too, do what Thorstein Veblen called “invidious comparisons”: measuring ourselves against others through social status, wealth display, educational attainment, and other markers of success. In The Theory of the Leisure Class , Veblen wrote of nineteenth-century consumers drawn to “pecuniary emulation”: competition through conspicuous consumption and the deployment of wealth as competitive display in and of itself. Invidious comparison is the habit of evaluating ourselves and others according to visible markers of luxury and ostentatiousness. The logic remains the same. The same forces run through the nineteenth century to the present. But the status jockeying of today takes place through social media, where personal brands and influencer aspirations fill all of our feeds. Who wants to labor when you can sell “content” instead? It’s tough to blame the dreamer. Survey the labor market, catch the stench of decay wafting up from late-stage capitalism, or remember that every moment of hope seems to be interrupted by wildfires, floods, and heat waves, and the question becomes almost unavoidable: “What else would you have people do? I mean, look at the state of the place .” Hyperpolitics and Reinstitutionalization Support for the critique itself provides an answer. Anton Jäger, author of Hyperpolitics , argues that a decline in institutionalization — cultures and norms of joining, especially among workers’ organizations — after 1989 has given way to runaway politicization without the roots established by gathering and belonging. In the space left by the death of institutionalization, hyperpolitics thrives while the customs of collective organization atrophy. The resulting loneliness and anomie make individualized escape — through personal branding and the like — seem more plausible than collective action. In tandem with the globalization of mass communication and a contemporary culture of instant gratification and attention, the rags-to-riches influencer dream seems a natural way to fill the void. It won’t. But reinstitutionalization would. Particularly as part of a greater movement to rebuild social trust and capital through strengthening offline social bonds and movements alongside worker-led (and owned) workplaces. On a social level, reconnecting with one another in the world, and democratizing opportunities to shape and run labor spaces, would provide greater meaning to both communities and work, encouraging a culture of dropping in — and staying for a while. It is also the only way to rebuild the institutions through which workers can recover their collective voice and power, pushing back against hyperpolitics and opening more space beyond work for each of us to create online and offline, to our heart’s content.

articles.title: M. N. Pokrovsky Pioneered Russia’s Marxist School of History
articles.author: James D. White
articles.content: Mikhail Nikolaevich Pokrovsky was the leading Soviet historian during the 1920s. He is credited with being the first person to present the history of Russia from a Marxist perspective. He was responsible for establishing the main academic institutions of the Soviet era, and for founding the leading historical journals. However, the Soviet authorities denounced Pokrovsky’s writings after his death in 1932, branding them as schematic and anti-Marxist. It was not until Joseph Stalin’s death in 1953 that Pokrovsky was rehabilitated and his chief works were republished. Education Pokrovsky was born in 1868 in Moscow, the son of a senior civil servant. He studied history at Moscow University, where the eminent scholars Vasily Klyuchevsky and Paul Vinogradov taught him. Klyuchevsky lectured on Russian history, while Vinogradov tackled ancient and European history. It was from these teachers that Pokrovsky derived his early approach to history. From Klyuchevsky, Pokrovsky learnt to appreciate the importance of the economic factor in shaping events, a phenomenon that he referred to as “economic materialism” and which he would later attribute to Karl Marx. In 1891, Pokrovsky graduated with a first-class diploma and eagerly accepted the offer to study for a postgraduate degree. After three years of intensive study that included both Russian history and the history of medieval Europe, he passed his master’s examination in 1894. The next step would have been to research for his master’s dissertation, which would have been presented as part of Pokrovsky’s formal training as an academic. However, this did not happen. Due to a disagreement with Klyuchevsky, Pokrovsky quit the university and went to teach history at an education college for girls. He nevertheless continued with his historical studies and was able to publish his first academic works in a multivolume collection of essays on European medieval history edited by Vinogradov. Vinogradov was an Anglophile liberal who subscribed to the positivist doctrine that all countries pass through the same historical stages. He believed that where England had gone, Russia would later follow — that is, to a system of parliamentary government. This was the historical and political credo that Pokrovsky espoused prior to the 1905 revolution, and his contributions to liberal publications reflected this outlook. 1905 Through his colleague the historian Nikolai Rozhkov, Pokrovsky made the acquaintance of Alexander Bogdanov , who in 1904 was ending his spell of banishment in Vologda for his activities in opposition to the tsarist regime. He contributed an article to the literary and philosophical journal Pravda that Bogdanov edited. When the 1905 revolution broke out, Pokrovsky participated in the literary lecturing group in Moscow that consisted of Bogdanov’s associates. Bogdanov himself led the Bolsheviks in St Petersburg. It was as a member of the literary lecturing group that Pokrovsky joined the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party (RSDLP). In June 1905, Pokrovsky traveled to Geneva and met Vladimir Lenin, who invited him to write an article for the party paper Proletarii . In it, Pokrovsky argued that liberals should not be alienated, because they could be won over to social democracy. Lenin did not agree. During the revolutionary events of 1905, Pokrovsky and the members of the literary lecturing group toured the Moscow region, giving lectures on behalf of the RSDLP and publishing a series of party newspapers. Even after the defeat of the December uprising in Moscow, Pokrovsky’s group attempted to continue the revolutionary struggle. Early Works and Exile In 1906, Pokrovsky published Economic Materialism , a pamphlet in which he outlined his views on how Marxist history should be written. In his view, the economic factor was paramount in explaining events. Personalities simply reflected the economic trends of the time, and material interests, reflected in the class struggle, were the driving force of history. According to Pokrovsky, there was no essential difference between Russian history and that of Western European countries. In 1907, Pokrovsky was forced to flee Russia and seek refuge in Finland, where he began to work on chapters for the nine-volume History of Russia in the XIX Century . Other chapters were contributed by fellow academics, members of the literary lecturing group, and representatives of the RSDLP, including Julius Martov . Pokrovsky’s approach in the chapters was almost entirely factual, with little sign that he had followed the principles embodied in Economic Materialism . In 1909, Pokrovsky moved to France, where he lived until the outbreak of the Russian Revolution in 1917. His main occupation in exile was writing the five-volume History of Russia from the Earliest Times . This was to be Pokrovsky’s main work, and he intended it to surpass in scholarship Klyuchevsky’s renowned Course of Russian History . The work plays down the role of individuals in history and tries to find economic explanations for events — for example, in the changes in grain prices. In his subsequent work Study in the History of Russian Culture , Pokrovsky finds a new driving force in Russian history: the struggle between merchant and industrial capital. Between the Revolutions In his period of exile, Pokrovsky came into political conflict with Lenin. It was Lenin’s contention that the revolutionary era was over with the failure of the 1905 revolution, and that the Bolshevik tactic must be support for the RSDLP faction in the Duma. Bogdanov, however, believed that the Duma faction should follow party policy, and if it did not, it should be served an ultimatum to do so. In the event of noncompliance, the faction should be recalled from the Duma. Bogdanov also considered that all the factors that had brought about the 1905 revolution were still in operation, and that a new revolutionary upsurge was in the offing. To prepare the workers for this renewal of the revolution, Bogdanov organized a party school on Capri in 1909 and one in Bologna in the following year. Pokrovsky sided with Bogdanov against Lenin, and gave lectures on Russian history at the Capri and Bologna party schools. When Lenin organized Bogdanov’s expulsion from the Bolshevik Center, Pokrovsky gave Bogdanov his support, but he then left Bogdanov’s Vpered group in 1911 over disagreements on proletarian culture. Pokrovsky, now outside both the Bolshevik and Menshevik factions of the RSDLP, found an ally in Leon Trotsky, who also stood outside both factions. Pokrovsky contributed to Trotsky’s publications Bor’ba and Nashe Slovo with articles on Russian history and foreign policy. Pokrovsky was a specialist on the history of Russian foreign policy, and in his works on the subject, he stressed Russia’s often aggressive stance. For example, he argued that Russia’s attempts to acquire Constantinople and the Turkish Straits in the interests of merchant capital had contributed to the outbreak of World War I. After 1914, Pokrovsky’s antiwar stance brought him closer to Lenin and the Bolsheviks. In 1916, he helped Lenin publish his pamphlet, Imperialism , the Highest Stage of Capitalism . Narkompros After the fall of tsarism in 1917, Pokrovsky returned to Russia and was active in the October revolution in Moscow. On Trotsky’s invitation, he went to Brest-Litovsk for peace negotiations with the Germans. However, he became disillusioned with Trotsky’s tactics, which depended entirely on fomenting revolution in Germany. As Anatoly Lunacharsky’s deputy at the Commissariat of Education (Narkompros), Pokrovsky was principally responsible for reorganizing the educational and cultural institutions of the new Soviet state. He organized and became chairman of the USSR Central Archives Administration. He founded the Socialist (later Communist) Academy, the Institute of Red Professors (IKP), the Association of Sciences Research Institutes (RANION), and the Society of Marxist Historians. Besides editing and contributing to a number of journals, Pokrovsky wrote the history textbook, the Brief History of Russia . In 1922, Pokrovsky’s interpretation of Russian history was challenged by the translation of Trotsky’s book 1905 , which had originally been published in German in 1909. In keeping with Trotsky’s theory of permanent revolution, 1905 insisted that Russia had no indigenous capitalist development and that its industry was entirely of foreign origin. A debate ensued in which Pokrovsky defended his idea that Russian tsarism was the embodiment of merchant capital. Trotsky’s opponents utilized his arguments in the contemporary anti-Trotsky campaign. A photo portrait of M. N. Pokrovsky published in 1930 by the State Publishing House. Pokrovsky’s standing as a historian began to be undermined in 1924 with the publication of Nikolai Bukharin’s essay “Lenin as Marxist,” which established the principle that all scholarship should be conducted from a Leninist viewpoint. Since Pokrovsky’s main works were pre-Soviet, his critics could condemn them as “anti-Leninist.” With the support of Stalin, however, he avoided this fate for the time being. Another difficulty for Pokrovsky arose in 1925 when a pupil of his at IKP, N. Vanag, published research showing that foreign capital controlled three-quarters of the whole Russian banking system on the eve of World War I. This meant that Russian monopoly capitalism was not an independent entity, but a component part of Anglo–French–Belgian finance capital. Vanag’s study was followed by others that reached the same conclusion. Pokrovsky initially accepted Vanag’s findings and adjusted his conception of modern Russian history accordingly. However, he later rejected this line of argument, since Vanag seemed to lend support to Trotsky’s version of Russian economic development. Death and Dishonor When Pokrovsky died in 1932, he was honored as an outstanding Soviet scholar. There was a proposal that Moscow University be renamed in his honor. A two-volume collection of his essays appeared in 1933, indicating official approval of his work, especially his polemic against Trotsky. But the anti-Pokrovsky campaign began soon afterward. Pokrovsky had assumed that the theory of “socialism in one country” would be bolstered by a version of Russian history that stressed indigenous economic development. In fact, what Stalin wanted was an interpretation of Russia’s past that focused on Russia’s weakness, its vulnerability to attack, and consequently its need for rapid industrial construction. That was why Stalin chose Vanag to edit a new textbook on Russian history, and he was disappointed when Vanag misunderstood his assignment. He rebuked Vanag for not showing Russia’s subservience to foreign finance capital. The 1938 Short Course of the RKP(b) , edited by Stalin himself, declared that the chain of imperialism had broken at its weakest link — Russia. In 1936, a campaign against Pokrovsky began in the pages of Pravda and Izvestia . Official polemicists accused him of writing history in abstract sociological terms and of denying the possibility of objective history. Quoting Pokrovsky out of context, his critics charged him with teaching that “history is politics projected into the past.” As an inverted tribute to Pokrovsky’s influence on Soviet scholarship, two volumes of anti-Pokrovsky essays were published in 1939–40 under the titles Against the Historical Conception of M. N. Pokrovsky (1939) and Against the Anti-Marxist Conception of M. N. Pokrovsky (1940). Among the contributors to the volumes were a number of Pokrovsky’s former students, including Anna Pankratova, who had previously written an effusive obituary of her teacher. Pankratova now denounced Pokrovsky as an associate of both Bogdanov and Trotsky, and as someone who had collaborated with spies and wreckers and had not been guided by Lenin’s works. For the rest of Stalin’s life, Soviet periodicals only mentioned Pokrovsky and his views in a negative light, as an example of how history should not be written. With Stalin’s death, however, and the accompanying “thaw,” Pokrovsky was rehabilitated. Assessing Pokrovsky Between 1965 and 1967, a four-volume edition of Pokrovsky’s selected works appeared in Moscow. It contained the History of Russia from the Earliest Times , the Brief History of Russia , and a collection of essays. A biography of Pokrovsky by O. D. Sokolov, who edited the selected works, was published in 1971. After the fall of the Soviet Union, a great many studies of Pokrovsky were completed, and some of his main works were republished. It is commonly said that Pokrovsky was a “Soviet historian” and that he was a “Marxist historian.” But these descriptions are not entirely appropriate. Pokrovsky’s chief works were written prior to 1917, and he resisted any pressure to align them with the Soviet ideological orthodoxy of the time. His critics were right when they said that he was not influenced by Lenin. But his writings show little sign that Marx was an influence either. There is, of course, Pokrovsky’s concern to discover an economic causation for the historical events he recounts, which may be taken for Marxism. But this approach comes less from Marx, than from Pokrovsky’s teachers Klyuchevsky and Vinogradov. Pokrovsky is in fact a Russian historian in the prerevolutionary tradition. While he is a major figure in the history of the Soviet Union, he also belongs to the history of Russian historiography more generally.

articles.title: Beheading the Hydra
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: Nexuses of electric eyes are the newest appendage of capitalism. There are now cities in the United States where, as a driver, your location is constantly tracked. This has happened quietly in the past few years, as technology costs decrease and private companies have secured the right to produce data from the public. The company that ruthlessly tracks drivers is called Flock. Campaigns to dismantle Flock contracts have brought tech critics and anti-capitalists together. But surveillance plays a strange, integral role in the current political economy, one that threatens to stabilize Flock when narrow criticisms against it are addressed. For example, in Eugene, OR, where a local Flock contract was dropped, the police department maintained that “while there were concerns about certain vulnerabilities and data security requirements with the particular vendor, the technology itself is not the problem.” Flock primarily sells Automated License Plate Reader cameras, which they set up at intersections and roadsides to fulfill their municipal contracts. It has become a shared target because a n open-source project scraped and published the location of Flock cameras across the country. It made them visible, and therefore targetable. Controversies over ICE’s use of Flock data and police stalking people using the same drew attention. Progressive nonprofits like Fight for the Future, the ACLU, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation waded in and started to mobilize people against the company. Socialists in Flagstaff, AZ, successfully campaigned to have their city council drop a contract with Flock. At the recent DSA Summit, de-Flock campaigns received enthusiastic attention as a way to constrain ICE’s prison archipelago. Surveillance is an extremely difficult topic to organize around, for reasons I will discuss later, so we should be glad this pattern has produced successful campaigns. But the focus on Flock means we are missing the larger picture—the surveillance industry as a whole. A survey of surveillance professionals found that most believe Flock creates problems for their entire industry. Already, executives are distancing themselves from Flock’s practices and finding ways to return to the comfort and obscurity of corporate self-regulation. If nothing is done, Flock will be marked as a solitary bad apple as the broader industry continues to spread the same kinds of tools and practices. To fight capital’s surveillance state, socialists will have to dig deeper and understand the contradictions it poses for our liberatory project. To explain this, I will start with the political economic reasons why increasing surveillance technology is part of the current base of production, which makes moral arguments against surveillance of limited use. I will then go into the moral arguments—centered around privacy—to demonstrate. In the end, I do not know the exact way to expand the fight against Flock. But I know it will require a conceptual shift, where we turn away from the individualistic legal-rights frameworks that have historically been popular for contesting surveillance tools. Instead, we need to imagine surveillance as a collective harm that will only be healed by collective care, for our neighbors, for our class. As more chapters adopt de-Flock campaigns as priorities, it is worthwhile for us to develop a deeper analysis of the harms that surveillance poses to the working class, its connections to US militarism abroad, and the limitations of prior efforts to end corporate and government surveillance. The Political Economy of Surveillance In the current phase of capitalism, data is capital. Like cultural or social capital, it can be exchanged at certain rates for economic capital. Information collection has always played a role in the accumulation of capital, from logging of productivity measurements and profits to financial journalism on market behaviors and ship deliveries. Information helps capitalists to navigate risks and produce profits out of an irrational economic system. Over time, however, the production of information has increased to such a point that we now see it in its most discrete, atomized form—data. Through the 20 th century, as the United States economy became defined by its excesses of consumption (Cohen 2004), marketers created techniques to produce desire within mass-media audiences. They learned, however, that isolating and targeting specific populations increased the power of their message, through tailoring. In his study of 1990s mass-mail marketing, scholar Oscar Gandy identified a growing economic form that he called “the panoptic sort, the all-seeing eye of the difference machine that guides the global capitalist system” (Gandy 2021). Marketers started hoarding personal consumer data to identify and target cohorts of consumers for personalized ad campaigns, to instill specific desires in specific sections of the population. The resulting panoptic sort produces discrimination and atomization, as individuals are made visible to capital via smaller and smaller distinctions. Corporations and their marketing departments created, as Gandy describes, “a kind of high-tech, cybernetic triage through which individuals and groups of people are being sorted according to their presumed economic or political value. The poor, especially poor people of color, are increasingly being treated as broken material or damaged goods to be discarded or sold at bargain prices to scavengers in the marketplace.” This panoptic sort then became the core of the 2010s tech boom, through surveillance advertising. Its success is, I believe, part of the reason we are living through a moment of proletarian disorganization . A scale of mass surveillance that would never have been permitted, if undertaken by the U.S. government, was applauded as the means through which tech companies could save a post-recession economy. This was the period where data finally became a driving element within capitalism, supported by state largesse. As Jathan Sadowski describes, “Fortunately for these companies, data capital, like financial capital, is treated as an engine of growth and epicenter of power and is thus governed by regimes of ‘light touch’ regulation, which are more interested in supporting than they are stymieing the smooth circulation of data capital” (Sadowski 2025, 84). Data has become a source of surplus value. Companies and capitalists are compelled to produce and accumulate as much data as possible. At the same time, the extreme overproduction of data to serve the panoptic sort overwhelmed human comprehension. Computers helped to store and retrieve this data. Disciplines like statistics and mathematics made it comprehensible to experts, but even they strained to put the vast supply to optimal use. So, computer science—that faithful, now discarded, squire of capital—produced algorithms that could credibly compress that data into new and exotic forms. This is all that large-language models and so-called “artificial intelligence” software are: tools for synthesizing insane quantities of data into something quickly comprehensible. Encyclopedias have done the same for centuries. But specifically for this story, these tools made the computational processing of image data comparatively cheap. The limiting factor on video surveillance up until recently was the price of guard or security labor. A networked camera that feeds data into an empty server does not perform surveillance, unless there is someone to watch and then use that data. (Data, like all other kinds of capital, is dead labor that must be revivified [Marx 2024].) But video analytics, notification, and search all expedite that watching. I recently heard a police chief describe this change, at a talk. Time was, if you knew of a store where someone you wanted to track had been, you had to go and collect physical VHS tapes and then use a fancy 2x playback feature so that it would take you 4 hours to watch an 8 hour video. Now, he said, “We can search all 42 cameras [of our video surveillance system] at once.” This is the automation of labor. That means, in a service economy, there is an economic incentive to adopt surveillance technologies—they replace, one by one, the labor of sworn and civilian cops. That pressure for adoption comes not just from within policing agencies but from their constituencies as well, who demand more information, more transparency, more efficiency. This same police chief was asked, after his talk, about pushback on his agency’s video surveillance system. He said it was not really a problem, because “ When a crime is committed, the first thing people ask is, where is the video?” By controlling the production of data about their activities, police also secure control of narratives about their crimes. Scholar Bryce Clayton Newell observed this effect in his study of the limited accountability created by body-worn camera programs: “Body-worn cameras are a state-supported, administrative response to bystander video and other forms of increasing police visibilities; as such, they support the police and legitimize official state narratives and the use of state police power” (Newell 2021). Copwatch programs put an effective check on police action, but one response by agencies has been to relocate video production within their own control and demanding the funding to do so. The US empire depends on a global chain of workers who have been pacified into productivity by dispossession, exploitation, and commodification: “To understand pacification is to understand how capitalism itself is produced and reproduced” (Rigakos 2022). And when data is capital, socialists need to understand how data subjects are pacified into playing a part in the production of data. Beyond its agencies themselves, the entire U.S. security state is a boon to the surveillance industry. Secured supply chains gather steel, copper, plastic, and Taiwanese semiconductors to manufacture cameras, cables, and servers that can navigate the US’ Dual-Use Technology Controls on their import and export. Security labor designs and installs surveillance assemblages grafted onto public housing, traffic lights, and signs. Software providers like Axon and Genentec design platforms that can synthesize private and public data sources in local fusion centers, Real-Time Crime Centers. The Department of Homeland Security funds private corporate actors and public agencies to create an “information sharing environment,” where grants are contingent on data-sharing collaborations with ICE via 287(g) agreements. Just as many of the academic grant-giving agencies have been gutted, DHS research and development arms are recreating the Cold War academy, to find new ways to pacify domestic populations. Where before surveillance advertising was able to isolate single consumers, video surveillance isolates individuals so they can be put into profit-driven camps and detention facilities. This is the scale of the enterprise that municipal Flock agreements are a part of. The Limits of Privacy Against this surveillant economic system, its opponents often march under the banners of privacy and Luddism. The current form these values take, however, is individual abstention from a system of social exploitation. Let me explain. For over a decade, “tech lash” activists have tried to curb the excesses of so-called surveillance capitalism. In so doing, they have often focused on privacy to explainas the harm it causes. While privacy is a changing social norm, it is usually parsed as a “right to be left alone.” This right, however, is legally derived from property. In fact, capitalism depends on an apparently clear division between public and private. That division allows private accumulation from previously public resources. The state continuously polices that boundary for the working class, even as it allows capital to smuggle public goods into private profit—a kind of osmosis. “The border between public and private spheres, that is, the myth of the autonomy of state and market, is particularly vehemently defended, for it is the cornerstone of liberal capitalism,” Micol Seigel (2016) argues in her history of US international police advisors. When Louis Brandeis and Samuel Warren (1890) first attempted to craft a doctrine on privacy out of constitutional and common law, they did so to keep photojournalists away from high society weddings. While they formulate privacy as the right to an “inviolate personality,” US law has developed through a combination of Fourth Amendment protections combined with civil tort cases to understand this right as particularly protecting expectations of privacy for one’s possessions. These are all subject to revocation by the state under “reasonable suspicion” but they also remain completely silent on the subject of the private accumulation of personal data. The scale of harm caused by massive data breaches can scarcely be estimated. And the “third-party doctrine” allows the government to do an end-run around any listed protections, by subpoenaing private companies—it simply deputizes data collection work to private companies. Against this, a range of technology nonprofits have offered their services. Borrowing countercultural aesthetics (Turner 2006), these nonprofits have made legal combat the primary venue through which surveillance issues are resolved. The law, however, is where the deck is stacked against the working class. Many of our movements have been quashed by the state via extralegal surveillance operations, like COINTELPRO. We do not own estates, gates, and guards to help us press a claim of violation. We do not have a court that will hear the mass collection of private data and issue a decree for jubilee. Further, privacy as individual enjoyment of property is a flimsy tool for building the subject of collective action—how can we imagine the place of privacy in class consciousness? In many cases, to build our consciousness as a class, we actually need to tear down the barriers that hide away inequality and injustice, like the feminist Wages for Housework movement. In others, we actually already understand publicity as the condition for supporting one another. Legal scholar Khiara Bridges has shown how US public welfare assumes the need for privacy violation, to provide social services to families (Bridges 2017). Flock, and the security industry, recognizes the flimsiness of relying on moral appeals against surveillance. They want to take it head-on. In a recently leaked media guide , Flock consultant Jamie Hudson advises, “Don’t avoid the concept of mass surveillance because you are not going to convince opponents that it’s not.” Instead, surveillance advocates and police departments are encouraged to focus on “governance.” That is, to emphasize how mass surveillance tools actually help towns appear to deliver services to their constituencies. At the same talk I mentioned before, a police chief recommended emphasizing that “we’re not here for immigration.” If that doesn’t work, police can “overload ’em with statistics” about how cameras help them to solve crimes. If that doesn’t work, emotional language: “Are you going to tell some affected family that their case shouldn’t be solved because of some contrived reason?” Under Flock’s guidance, surveillance is a “force multiplier” that helps wise, frugal city councils efficiently fund their poor, cash-starved police departments. The reasoning is economic. It is meant to appear practical. And if Flock doesn’t succeed in this framing, there are plenty of other companies that will try. Stanford University, for example, has already replaced its Flock contract with a similar vendor of license-plate readers, Genetec. Conclusion The role of privacy in a socialist state is far from clear. Privacy grants space for the creation of the self. In US society, this is driven to an unnatural height, where people are both atomized and paranoid of surveillance. Profits from data extraction and analysis link the United States to Israel, which as a client-state service trades its war machines and surveillance technology tested on Palestinians (Al-Khatib et al. 2026). But collection of information, especially for industry, is just as part of socialist states as capitalist ones, as examples like the Chilean Project Cybersyn show. Our problem is not that data is collected at all; our question is not whether we should or should not. Our problem is that data is capital. Its accumulation is an economic imperative that shackles society to narrow, repressive strictures. Surveillance data production feeds the war machine and the private prison industry. That is what we need to change. Our question is how. Socialists have to build the alternative, especially when they are able to govern. Other countries, like the United Kingdom , have explored the creation of data trusts, where contributions are voluntary and benefits must be communal. Indigenous communities are exerting data sovereignty to block flows of data and extractive access to communal knowledge. Hackers and designers make technologies that evade or reconstruct the frictionless data environment we have come to see as natural, inevitable. Still, critiques of surveillance and aesthetics of resistance remain stuck in the age of Orwell’s 1984 and its surveillant television, itself a criticism of imperial British mass media society. But the beast has changed, and so must we. DeFlock, like Tesla Takedown before it, has shown that technology companies are just as vulnerable to pressure campaigns as any other. DeFlock goes a step further by targeting the source of funding for surveillance, where Tesla Takedown focused on changing public perception. But our horizon must be broader. Let us see surveillance for what it is—a part of capitalism. References Al-Khatib, Islam, Arees Bishara, Sarah Fathallah, et al. 2026.
